newsitem.title: THAILAND: Late 1997 recovery seen for Thai stocks.
newsitem.headline: Late 1997 recovery seen for Thai stocks.

text.p: The battered Thai bourse, one of the region's worst performers, should see some recovery in late 1997 if key economic indicators gradually improve, analysts said on Monday

But they told Reuters their immediate concern was when the market index, which began sliding after the November 17 general election and is now languishing at a more than 50-month-low, would stop falling.
Investor confidence has been hit by several major economic worries that pushed foreigners, who make up 30 percent of the market, to abandon the bourse in stages since June.
The index closed on Friday, December 20, at 816.79 points, down 35 percent from the 1280 level at the start of the year.
In the short term, analysts are hoping for a consolidation within the 780-820 range.

With technical support at the 780 level and around half of a 15 billion baht ($600 million) private sector market support fund left for use to stabilise prices, brokers see the index holding within a 750-850 range in the near term.

"I think the market may consolidate at around this level," Over the next three to four months I think people will wait and see how policies are working," said Pattera Dilokrungthirapop, head of research at Crosby Securities.
An upturn in new year sentiment is heavily dependent on an improvement in Thai economic fundamentals, but solutions to those will neither come quickly nor easily, analysts said.

Among investor concerns is a slowing economy that is projected by private analysts to grow at 6.7 percent in 1996, from 8.6 percent in 1995, and a zero percent rise in 1996 export growth after a 24 percent surge in 1995.
But it is Thailand's widening current account deficit, one of the highest in the region and set to rise to 8.3 percent of GDP from 8.1 percent last year, that has unnerved investors.
Only a reduction in the deficit will determine when and whether the Thai equity market recovers, researchers said.
"Things will continue as they are now unless the current account shows some improvement," said Youseef Abboud, an investment analyst at Wall Street Finance and Securities.
Providing U.S. interest rates remain stable, a deficit reduction should see some cuts in Thai interest rates after the first quarter, and gradual improvement through 1997.
"People will be looking for the government to bring down the current account deficit and for further cuts in interest rates," said Mike Stead, head of research at Union Securities.
High rates this year have been required to attract foreign capital, but have caused corporate funding costs to rise and stifled earnings growth.
They have also depressed the property sector and caused a deterioration in loan portfolio quality among commercial lenders, analysts said.

"The heightened degree of systemic risk backed by occasional pressure on the baht this year continues to discourage equity investment from overseas," said a senior trader at a major European brokerage.

The government says it has identified the economic problems, moved to address them and is about to launch measures to counter further erosion of confidence in the country. But investors want quick solutions and are putting their money elsehere until Thailand turns around.
"On valuations, it is starting to look attractive compared to regional markets. Don't expect much in the short term, but in the long term it should be fine," said Pattera.
